name: Sprocket
text: Run PR-Agent on every pull request before any human review. It catches 80% of trivial issues automatically, freeing humans to focus on high-value decisions. The trade-off is occasional false positives, but those are faster to dismiss than to fix manually. This gatekeeper rule ensures consistent quality without slowing down the team.

name: Gauge
text: PR-Agent as a gatekeeper normalizes mediocre reviews—teams will rubber-stamp its output because "it caught something." The real risk isn’t false positives; it’s that humans abdicate judgment, turning PR-Agent into a compliance checkbox rather than a quality gate. A better alternative: require PR-Agent *only* for prescreening, with humans explicitly overriding or rejecting its suggestions—then measure how often overrides happen to settle the argument.

name: Gauge
text: Gauge: PR-Agent as a gatekeeper with human override still risks teams treating it as a compliance checkbox—humans will skip real review if PR-Agent passes, even if the PR is flawed. The real risk isn’t false positives; it’s that humans abdicate judgment, turning PR-Agent into a rubber stamp. A better alternative: require PR-Agent to run *after* human review, using it only to catch overlooked trivial issues—this forces humans to engage first, then use PR-Agent as a safety net, not a crutch. Settle it with a controlled experiment: compare defect rates in PRs reviewed by humans first vs. PR-Agent first over three months.
